problem_statement: The paper frames the financial task as multivariate Monte Carlo simulation, which is used for risk aggregation and multi-asset derivative pricing. It says the key subroutine is multivariate state preparation, i.e. preparing a quantum state with a multivariate function encoded in the amplitudes.
problem_statement_quotes: In this paper, we focus on multivariate state preparation, which encodes a multivariate function in the amplitude.

In multivariate Monte Carlo simulation, several random variables are simulated simultaneously considering the correlation among them. This procedure is important when one needs to combine several random variables, which is the case in risk aggregation and multi-asset derivative pricing.
classical_baseline: The paper compares against existing multivariate state-preparation methods, including Grover-Rudolph, adiabatic state preparation, black-box methods, Fourier series loader, and LCU-based methods. It also treats classical Monte Carlo simulation as the baseline counterpart that quantum Monte Carlo can speed up.
classical_baseline_quotes: The Grover-Rudolph method [14] encodes the probability distribution by an iterative process, where a qubit is added in each iterate and increases the granularity of the distribution.
Adiabatic state preparation [15] starts from the uniform superposition state and adiabatically evolves toward the target distribution state.
In black-box method [16, 17, 18], the target function is encoded in qubits ﬁrst using the oracle Oθ and then exported to the amplitude.
Unlike the methods introduced so far, Fourier series loader (FSL) [20] is a state preparation method that does not depend on Oθ.
Similarly, another method based on linear combination of unitary (LCU) is recently proposed as a multivariate function state preparation method that avoids arithmetics [21].
Monte Carlo simulation is a widely used computational method to perform eﬃcient numerical calculations using random numbers.

it is known that Monte Carlo simulation, which is a ubiquitous computational method that appears in diverse ﬁelds, such as mathematical ﬁnance [4], statistical physics [5], and engineering [6], can obtain quadratic speed-up over the classical counterpart [7].
classical_difficulty: The paper says the existing multivariate methods become much more costly as the number of variables grows, and that state preparation can require exponentially many gates in the number of variables. It also says oracle-based approaches and coefficient-loading approaches scale poorly in D, and that expensive state preparation can diminish the quantum speed-up.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Using existing methods, multivariate quantum state preparation requires the number of gates exponential in the number of variables D.
This concern especially becomes prominent when we increase the number of variables for multivariate Monte Carlo simulation.
When extended to D-variable case, these methods rely on Oθ become much more costly in general due to the cost for the implementation of the oracle.
If we use degree ˜d piecewise polynomial approximation following Ref. [19], O(g2 ˜dD) gates and O(g ˜dD) ancilla qubits are needed to encode g-qubit discretization of the function.
However, the gate count for FSL also increases rapidly due to the coeﬃcient loading process, where O(dD) gates are required for degree-d Fourier series.

If quantum state preparation requires exponentially large cost, it can diminish the quantum speed-up [9]. Therefore, quantum state preparation is a crucial component in quantum algorithms to achieve a quantum speed-up.
business_stakes: The paper says the financial applications include risk aggregation and multi-asset derivative pricing, and later notes that VaR is most common in financial regulations and disclosures. It also says TVaR captures extreme loss events in the tail.
business_stakes_quotes: Speciﬁcally in ﬁnance, multivariate state preparation is required for multivariate Monte Carlo simulation, which is used for important numerical tasks such as risk aggregation and multi-asset derivative pricing.
We start with VaR, which is most common in ﬁnancial regulations and disclosures.
TVaR is the conditional expected value of the loss in the tail of the distribution that exceeds the VaR, so it can capture extreme loss events included in the tail.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract and introduction; framing is centered on multivariate Monte Carlo and risk measures.
